A fresco is a painting made directly on a wall or ceiling — but not just any wall painting. What makes a fresco unique and special is how it is made: the paint is applied onto wet plaster, not a dry surface. This single detail changes everything about what a fresco is, how it's made, and why it has survived for centuries.
The Core Idea: Paint Fused Into the Wall

In most paintings (think of a canvas painting hanging in a home), the paint sits on top of a surface. It can crack, peel, or fade over time.

A fresco works differently. When an artist paints onto freshly laid, still-wet plaster using water-mixed pigments (colors), something remarkable happens as the plaster slowly dries and hardens: the pigment doesn't just rest on the surface — it gets chemically absorbed and locked into the plaster itself. The color becomes part of the wall, almost like it has fused with it at a molecular level.

The result is a painting that is essentially as permanent as the wall it's on. It won't peel. It won't flake off. It becomes inseparable from the structure of the building.

Making a fresco requires extreme skill and careful planning. Here's how the process works:

  1. A section of the wall is first given a rough base coat of plaster and left to dry.
  2. The artist then applies a fresh, thin top coat of smooth, wet plaster — but only over a small area, because this wet plaster is the working surface, and it has a very short lifespan.
  3. The artist has only a few hours — sometimes as little as two to six hours — to paint on that section before the plaster dries and hardens completely.
  4. Once dry, no more paint can be absorbed. That section is finished forever.
  5. The next day, the artist plasters a new small section and paints that. This continues day by day until the entire wall or ceiling is complete.

This is why each day's painted section is called a giornata, an Italian word for "a day's work." Historians who study old frescoes can sometimes detect the faint seam lines between each giornata, essentially reading the diary of how the artist worked.
Why This Makes It So Difficult

Because the plaster dries so fast, the artist cannot take their time. There is no "paint a little, step back, think, come back tomorrow." Once you paint a stroke, it is permanent almost instantly. You cannot paint over it and fix it. If you make a serious mistake, the only solution is to chip off that section of plaster entirely, let the wall dry, and start that area over from scratch.

This means the artist must plan every detail of the composition in advance — the full design must be worked out on paper or on a smaller sketch before a single stroke touches the wall. The design is often transferred to the wall using a cartoon (a full-sized drawing on paper) that is pressed against the fresh plaster to leave an outline, which the artist then paints within.

Additionally, the range of colors (pigments) an artist can use in a fresco is limited. Many pigments react badly with wet lime plaster and either change color or get destroyed by it. Fresco artists had to work within a specific palette of lime-safe colors, which is why many old frescoes have that characteristic earthy, muted, yet richly harmonious color feel.
The Two Main Types of Fresco

While "fresco" broadly means a wall painting, there are two specific forms:

1. Buon fresco ("true fresco")
This is what is described above — painting on wet plaster. This is the real, classical, and most celebrated form. It is the most durable because the pigment bonds chemically with the plaster.

2. Fresco secco ("dry fresco")
In this method, the artist paints on plaster that has already dried. To make the paint stick, a binding agent (such as egg, glue, or limewater) is mixed with the pigment. The result looks similar but is far less durable — the paint sits on top of the dry plaster rather than fusing into it, so it is far more likely to flake, chip, or deteriorate over time. Many ancient frescoes have lost sections that were painted secco while the sections painted in buon fresco remain intact.

The most celebrated frescoes in the world come from the Italian Renaissance (roughly the 1300s–1500s), when the technique reached its absolute peak.

  • The Sistine Chapel ceiling in Vatican City, painted by Michelangelo between 1508 and 1512, is the most famous fresco in the world. Michelangelo painted it lying on scaffolding high above the ground, covering over 500 square meters of ceiling with hundreds of figures — all in buon fresco.
  • The School of Athens by Raphael, also in the Vatican, is another landmark Renaissance fresco — a sweeping philosophical scene depicting the great thinkers of ancient Greece.
  • The Arena Chapel (Scrovegni Chapel) in Padua, Italy, decorated entirely with frescoes by Giotto di Bondone in the early 1300s, is considered a turning point in Western art history.

But frescoes are not only Italian or from the Renaissance. The ancient Romans painted frescoes in the homes and buildings of Pompeii (buried by the eruption of Mount Vesuvius in 79 AD and preserved almost perfectly). The ancient Minoans of Crete created stunning frescoes over 3,000 years ago. Medieval churches across Europe are filled with fresco paintings of biblical scenes, painted as a way to tell religious stories to populations that could not read.

Before printing, photography, or any form of mass communication existed, frescoes were one of the most powerful tools humans had for communicating stories, beliefs, history, and beauty on a grand scale. A fresco painted on the wall of a church could be seen by an entire community for generations. It was public art in its truest sense.

Their permanence also makes them incredibly valuable to historians. Because the pigment is locked into the plaster, properly preserved frescoes give us a direct, undistorted window into the colors, aesthetics, stories, and skills of civilizations long gone.

A fresco is a wall or ceiling painting in which water-mixed pigments are applied to wet plaster, permanently bonding with it as it dries, making the painting part of the wall itself. It is one of the oldest, most demanding, and most enduring art forms in human history — requiring mastery of planning, speed, chemistry, and artistic skill all at once.
